papers.title: [Editorial] Peripheral arterial disease: counting what matters
papers.summary: Peripheral arterial disease, caused by atherosclerotic narrowing of the arteries supplying the limbs, is widely regarded as a local disease of the legs and, particularly when asymptomatic, as relatively benign. Both impressions are inaccurate. Peripheral arterial disease is a manifestation of systemic atherosclerosis, and when symptoms do appear, they are often attributed to ageing or musculoskeletal disease, and only a minority of patients report the classical intermittent claudication—exertional leg pain relieved by rest—that clinicians are taught to search for.

papers.title: [Comment] Combining immunotherapy with stereotactic body radiation therapy in localised non-small-cell lung cancer
papers.summary: Radiotherapy and immunotherapy combination has been a field of intense investigation globally over the past decade. The phase 3 randomised clinical trial (SWOG/NRG S1914) in The Lancet by Megan E Daly and colleagues,1 conducted in the USA, evaluated whether adding perioperative atezolizumab (neoadjuvant, concurrent, and adjuvant) to stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) improved outcomes in high-risk, medically inoperable early-stage non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Its primary objective was to compare overall survival between patients assigned to atezolizumab plus SBRT (n=210) or SBRT alone (n=207).

papers.title: [Comment] The US experiments with international reference pricing for prescription drugs
papers.summary: The USA pays substantially more for the same branded drug compared with other high-income nations, with estimates suggesting the USA pays three to five times the price compared with most European countries.1 For many, including the Trump administration, these higher prices represent an unfairness in the global pharmaceutical market. In his first term, US President Donald Trump directed the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Innovation (CMMI) to benchmark Medicare part B drug prices to international prices as a form of international reference pricing.

papers.title: [Comment] Can wealth redistribution offset the collapse of aid?
papers.summary: Official development assistance (ODA) is being cut faster than at any point in history.1 The USA, the UK, Japan, Germany, France, and the Netherlands have all reduced aid between 2024 and 2025, and forecasts point to further large declines up to and after 2026.1 These cuts are occurring within the backdrop of extreme and rising wealth concentration: the richest 10% of the world's population own 75% of global personal wealth, whereas the poorest 50% own just 2%.2 Considering this fact, in The Lancet Gonzalo Barreix Sibils and colleagues ask a largely unexamined question: could redistributing even a small share of that wealth offset the health damage caused by the humanitarian and development aid crisis?3

papers.title: [Comment] Compassionate care for patients with Ebola virus disease
papers.summary: The current Ebola virus outbreak, caused by Bundibugyo virus (BDBV), in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DR Congo) is expanding rapidly and is the second largest Ebola epidemic in history.1 By Sept 6, 2026, there were 6686 confirmed cases including 3226 deaths (crude case-fatality ratio 48·3%).2 Health-care workers have also been heavily affected: 167 health-care workers were confirmed to have had BDBV in DR Congo by Sept 6, 2026, of whom 47 had died (case-fatality ratio 28·1%)2 and by Aug 9 the same year, 68 health-care workers had recovered.

papers.title: [Comment] High-quality mentorship can improve physician-scientist recruitment, retention, and career satisfaction
papers.summary: Physician-scientists, who engage in both patient care and scientific inquiry, represent an increasingly small portion of the physician workforce. In the USA, only 1·3% of physicians reported research as their major professional activity in 2020.1 In the UK, clinical academics represented just 3·2% of the consultant workforce in 2025.2

papers.title: [Comment] Offline: Can time be tamed?
papers.summary: When Evan Hubinger, a safety scientist at Anthropic, posted on X last month that there is a greater than 10% chance that artificial intelligence (AI) could kill all humans within the next decade, he was making a prophecy of eye-catching proportions. Medicine is the discipline among all disciplines that knows something about prophecies. Doctors learn the natural history of disease to guide patients through the likely course of their illness. Clinical researchers do randomised trials to make judgements about the safety and efficacy of the treatments they prescribe.

On both occasions, the port designated by the Italian authorities for the disembarkation of the rescued individuals required the ship to sail for several days to ports in northern Italy. After the first operation, a voyage of more than 700 nautical miles to the port of Savona transformed the deck of the Open Arms from an emergency scene into a place of waiting.

papers.title: [Correspondence] From isolation to burial: dignity in the Bundibugyo virus disease response

papers.title: [Correspondence] Multicancer detection tests: holy grail or cautionary tale?
papers.summary: A single blood test that can identify most cancers remains the aspirational goal of cancer screening. The US biotechnology company Grail has been closest to developing a viable multicancer detection test. In June, 2026, the high hopes of many were dashed at the annual American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO) scientific meeting: Grail's landmark Galleri trial, which randomly assigned 140 000 UK residents to usual care plus multicancer detection testing versus usual care alone, failed to meet its primary endpoint—a reduction in late-stage cancers.

We, however, believe that the central issue extends beyond vancomycin-resistant enterococci.

papers.title: [Series] Understanding peripheral arterial disease in the current era
papers.summary: Atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease is the primary driver of premature death in global populations in recent decades. Mortality statistics, most publications, and guidelines in the atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease field have traditionally focused on cardiac and cerebrovascular adverse events and causes of death. However, given the increasing prevalence of lower extremity peripheral arterial disease and its expanding burden on global health systems, such an emphasis might represent a skewed perception of vascular risk within the broader atherosclerotic spectrum.

papers.title: [Series] Current advancements in the care of peripheral arterial disease: modern approaches to medical, endovascular, and surgical treatment
papers.summary: People with peripheral arterial disease (PAD) of the lower limbs are at very high risk of cardiovascular events and therefore the cornerstone of their management is medical therapy and behaviour modification to reduce that risk. The risk of limb loss (through major amputation) is low in people with asymptomatic PAD or intermittent claudication with only a few patients progressing to the most severe form of PAD: chronic limb threatening ischaemia. Supervised exercise therapy is effective in patients with intermittent claudication to improve their walking capacity and avoids the risks associated with revascularisation procedures to improve blood flow to the limb.

papers.title: [Series] Peripheral arterial disease: adverse impacts, disparities in outcomes, and the path ahead
papers.summary: This is the third paper in the peripheral arterial disease (PAD) Series. The first and second papers in this Series outline that PAD affects over 300 million people worldwide and can be diagnosed by non-invasive tests, as well as that treatment requires medications to reduce modifiable risk factors and that exercise therapy and revascularisation are required in selected patients. In this paper, the devastating effects of PAD at the individual level are described, including chronic pain, functional limitation, loss of independence, impaired physical and mental quality of life, unemployment, and financial instability.

papers.title: [Editorial] Counteracting the rise of antimicrobial resistance in Shigella
papers.summary: Shigella, a Gram-negative bacterium, causes shigellosis, characterised by intestinal symptoms. Shigellosis is one of the leading causes of global diarrhoeal disease deaths, especially in children younger than 5 years. Shigella disproportionately affects low-income and middle-income countries (LMICs), where transmission occurs mainly through the oral–faecal route due to poor water, sanitation, and hygiene practices. Shigella is divided into four main species: S dysenteriae, S boydii, S flexneri, and S sonnei, of which all have multiple serotypes except S flexneri.

papers.title: [Comment] South Sudan's first 100 days of Bundibugyo Ebola readiness
papers.summary: When the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DR Congo) and Uganda declared an outbreak of Ebola virus disease caused by Bundibugyo virus (BDBV) on May 15, 2026, South Sudan looked likely to be the next country affected. Modelling estimated a 70% probability that at least one case would cross into the country within 12 weeks,1 driven by intense population movement across porous borders with DR Congo and Uganda. The amplifiers that have propelled the epidemic in the Ituri province—armed conflict, displacement, and a fragile health system—are at least as pronounced in South Sudan, and pathogens do not respect borders.

papers.title: [Correspondence] Cross-reactive Bundibugyo antibody responses in Guinean survivors of Ebola virus and recipients of rVSVΔG-ZEBOV-GP (Ervebo) in an outbreak setting
papers.summary: Control of the ongoing outbreak of Bundibugyo virus (BDBV) in DR Congo, already the largest on record, has been hindered by the absence of licensed vaccines. Although BDBV-specific vaccines are under development, the licensed and stockpiled Ebola virus vaccine (rVSVΔG-ZEBOV-GP; Ervebo, Merck Sharp & Dohme) warrants evaluation as a potential stopgap measure, particularly for those at high exposure risk (eg, front-line responders, health-care workers, and contacts). rVSVΔG-ZEBOV-GP has conferred partial heterologous protection against BDBV challenge in non-human primates,1,2 and mixed BDBV responses have been detected in west African3 and Congolese participants4 receiving this vaccine.

papers.title: [News] Research in brief
papers.summary: A cohort study in France assessed the monoclonal antibody nirsevimab against respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) in infants at 1 year and 2 years after immunisation. Outcomes were examined in infants born before the first RSVpreF vaccination campaign for pregnant women started in September 2024. Nirsevimab was associated with lower rates of RSV-lower respiratory tract-related hospitalisations during the first year after immunisation: 299 (0·8%) of 37 366 immunised versus 899 (2·4%) of 37 366 non-immunised infants in 2023, and 456 (0·5%) of 87 763 immunised versus 1711 (1.9%) of 87 763 non-immunised infants in 2024 (weighted hazard ratios 0·34, 95% CI 0·30–0·39 for the 2023 cohort and 0·28, 0.25–0·31 for the 2024 cohort, corresponding to nirsevimab effectiveness estimates of 66% and 72%, respectively).

She retired as Professor of Infectious Diseases at TUMS in 2022 and but continues in clinical practice in Tehran.

However, because his symptoms persisted, he was referred for further investigation. Colonoscopy revealed a circumferential 50 mm volcano-like rectal ulcer with an irregular, thick heaped-up margin and a deep ulcer base (figure A), accompanied by a smaller shallow round ulcer.

papers.summary: Pancreatic cancer cachexia is accompanied by progressive assembly of a spatially organized tumor-macrophage-fibroblast niche. Reciprocal signaling among the cellular populations in the niche is associated with muscle wasting and cachexia progression.

papers.title: Microbiome signatures linked to cancer and treatment adverse events in a real-world cohort

Distinct associations are limited to a subset of cancers and, in separate analyses, to age of onset and specific treatment-related adverse events.

papers.summary: Gut microbial taxonomy alone is a poor predictor of CAR-T cell therapy outcome. papers.summary: In-cell cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) combined with proteomics, integrative structural modeling, and bioinformatics enables discovery and functional annotation of uncharacterized proteins. In the minimal bacterium Mycoplasma pneumoniae, this reveals a complex that links Sec-based protein translocation and extracellular folding, capable of supporting both co- and post-translational pathways.

papers.title: Single-cell visual proteomics of a minimal bacterium reveals structural coordination of gene expression machineries
papers.summary: Cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) resolves and quantifies an almost complete view of bacterial translation, revealing how gene expression machineries coordinate across the processes of transcription, translation, and membrane engagement directly within a minimal bacterium.

papers.summary: Resident tissue macrophages establish a selenium-rich niche at the pancreatic tumor border and protect invading tumor cells from ferroptosis by transferring Selenop protein to EMThi cancer cells.

papers.title: A pericyte-to-myofibroblast transition links APOE4 to cerebrovascular degeneration
papers.summary: APOE4 causes a pericyte-to-myofibroblast transition that promotes cerebrovascular fibrosis and perivascular amyloid accumulation. TGF-β inhibition reverses this pathological remodeling and thus presents a therapeutic strategy to restore cerebrovascular homeostasis in these high-risk individuals.

papers.title: Shifts in embryonic oxygen levels cue heterochrony in limb initiation
papers.summary: Mammalian embryos see a substantial increase in available oxygen once the placenta forms. This increase in oxygen exposure serves as a trigger for initiating the development of the hindlimb, thus controlling developmental timing and, more broadly, linking the maternal environment to evolutionary changes in body plan.

papers.title: Microbial signaling coordinates group oviposition and predator defense in migratory locusts
papers.summary: This study reveals an egg-associated bacterial signaling mechanism that couples reproductive synchronization with offspring defense in the locust L. migratoria, expanding the functional landscape of insect-microbe-predator interactions and demonstrating how microbial signals can shape complex ecological behaviors.

papers.title: Direct cell-to-cell transmission of retrotransposons
papers.summary: Retrotransposons can infect neighboring cells using a mechanism that relies on a small fusogen-like protein rather than on the envelope protein that is typically required for infection.

papers.title: Projection-defined modules reveal mouse motor cortex architecture
papers.summary: The mouse motor cortex divides into 16 spatially organized modules based on distinct subcortical projections. This specificity covaries with cortical connectivity patterns and cell-type composition along two spatial axes, thereby defining the rules by which motor cortex modules integrate with granularity into brainwide and precisely wired neuronal networks to influence movement.

papers.title: CD4 T cells convert transient responses to KRAS inhibition to durable remissions in pancreatic cancer
papers.summary: An AI-designed IL-21 mimetic converts transient KRAS inhibitor responses into durable pancreatic cancer remissions through CD4 T cells, independent of CD8 T cells and tumor MHC class I expression.

papers.title: Switching of transcriptional control from interferon regulatory factor 2 to interferon regulatory factor 1 drives innate immune cell activation
papers.summary: Toll-like receptor signaling activates proinflammatory interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) even in the absence of interferon by triggering a shift from IRF2 to IRF1 occupancy at ISG promoters and enhancers. Newly translated IRF1 promotes proteasomal degradation of the weaker transcriptional activator IRF2 by engaging the E3 ubiquitin ligase SPOP.

papers.title: Chloroplasts balance energy production and stress resilience via a cold-induced signaling pathway
papers.summary: Cold-stress signals are transmitted to chloroplasts and subsequently trigger cold responses through an RAF-like bi-kinase module where cytoplasmic RAF3 and plasma membrane RAF6 translocate to chloroplasts, where they inhibit photosynthetic activity but activate nuclear cold-responsive gene expression.

papers.title: mRNA-encoding CD19-targeting T cell engager for refractory immune thrombocytopenia
papers.summary: An mRNA-lipid nanoparticle-encoded CD19×CD3 T cell engager depletes B cells with attenuated cytokine release in preclinical models. In three patients with treatment-refractory immune thrombocytopenia, treatment with this T cell engager achieved sustained platelet recovery over 6 months, suggesting that mRNA-encoded T cell engagers represent a promising therapeutic approach for resetting autoreactive immunity in B cell-driven autoimmune disease.

papers.title: Toward autonomous science with agentic artificial intelligence
papers.summary: Biomedical artificial intelligence is advancing from tools that answer human-posed questions to agents that ask their own. Guo et al. assess this transition, including scaling logic, autonomous-laboratory trajectory, and the risks of hallucination, bias, dual use, and cognitive deskilling. This perspective argues that progress depends on responsible human-AI collaboration.

papers.title: Phosphate backbone epitranscriptomics: Discovery of natural RNA phosphorothioates and their writer machinery
papers.summary: Phosphorothioates, stereospecific modifications of the RNA phosphate backbone in anaerobic archaea, expand the epitranscriptome beyond nucleobases and ribose sugars. Installed by Esti enzymes at conserved rRNA and tRNA hotspots, these environmentally responsive marks stabilize tRNAs and support growth at high temperatures.

papers.title: 3D chromatin remodeling during domestication defines novel targets for crop improvement
papers.summary: Population-level 3D genome atlas of 34 semi-wild and 267 cultivated allotetraploid cottons reveals domestication-selected chromatin conformations that enhance cotton fiber quality and unlock cryptic breeding targets.

papers.title: Gliomas phenocopy an inborn error of metabolism to drive neuronal activity and tumor growth
papers.summary: Glioma-derived guanidinoacetate depolarizes neighboring neurons through γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) A receptors, and depleting this metabolite reduces both neuronal activity and glioma growth.

papers.title: Single-cell-resolved genome atlas of prokaryoplankton inhabiting the ocean’s interior
papers.summary: GORG-Dark presents genomes of 9,698 individual bacterial and archaeal cells from the ocean’s sunless interior. The atlas resolves depth stratification to abyssal waters, uncovers particle-attached Pelagibacterales, maps chemolithoautotrophy and biosynthetic gene clusters, and identifies a rhodopsin clade specific to the dark ocean.

papers.title: Programmed ribosomal frameshifting triggers translational stress to promote viral replication
papers.summary: Viruses such as SARS-CoV-2 can use programmed ribosomal frameshifting to turn off host translation and promote viral replication, expanding the known uses of programmed ribosomal frameshifting by viruses.

papers.title: Norway spruce spatiotemporal programs of conifer reproductive development
papers.summary: Spatiotemporal transcriptomics across conifer reproductive and vegetative shoots reveals candidate developmental regulators and evolutionarily conserved tissue patterning genes in seed plants.

papers.title: Copper ion-induced MYH9 polymerization executes cuproptosis
papers.summary: Copper binding drives MYH9 polymerization, triggering cytoskeletal collapse and cuproptosis. HThPA releases intracellular copper through glutathione depletion, exposing a therapeutic vulnerability in drug-resistant tumors.

papers.title: Metax enables accurate cross-domain taxonomic profiling of metagenomes
papers.summary: Metax is a cross-domain metagenomic profiler that uses genome-wide coverage evidence to improve species-level microbial profiling and distinguish supported taxa from artifacts. Across diverse datasets, Metax enables robust taxonomic profiling, pathogen detection, contamination assessment, and discovery of disease-associated bacterial and viral signatures.

papers.title: Mitochondrial ATP promotes T cell differentiation through chromatin accessibility
papers.summary: Cell-mediated immunity requires cytotoxic CD8+ T cells that adopt and maintain an effector phenotype. Here, D-α-hydroxybutyrate (DAHB) is shown to act as a metabolic adjuvant, driving the conversion of proliferating CD8+ T cells into cytotoxic effector cells by linking mitochondrial ATP production to chromatin remodeling and gene expression.

papers.title: Glycocalyx-edited mesenchymal stem/stromal cell therapy in advanced osteoporosis
papers.summary: Mesenchymal stem/stromal cell (MSC)-based therapy holds promise for reversal of bone loss in osteoporosis. This phase 1 study establishes the safety and feasibility of intravenous administration of glycocalyx-engineered human MSCs and provides evidence that MSCs derived from the bone marrow of older individuals with osteoporosis retain clinically meaningful osteoregenerative capacity.

papers.title: Architecture of the serotonergic projectome in the mouse brain
papers.summary: Serotonin neurons innervate nearly the entire mammalian brain, yet how their projections are organized has remained unclear. Systematic whole-brain serotonergic axon collateralization mapping reveals five projectomic groups that preferentially target functionally related regions, with each projectomic group connecting to specific spatial transcriptomic and behavioral profiles.

papers.title: Caloric restriction modulates genome-wide somatic mutation in mice
papers.summary: Mutations accumulate in cells with age, while caloric restriction extends lifespan across diverse animals. Grońska-Pęski et al. study the effect of caloric restriction on mutations genome-wide in mice, finding reduced mutation burdens across several tissues and cell types, thereby establishing that diet can alter mutation accumulation genome-wide during aging.

papers.title: Structural basis of a SWI/SNF-associated transcription pre-initiation complex
papers.summary: Cryo-EM and genetic analyses reveal that the SWI/SNF chromatin remodeler is an integral component of the transcription pre-initiation complex. The structures demonstrate how SWI/SNF facilitates transcription initiation through stabilization of PIC organization and concerted remodeling of the +1 nucleosome.

papers.title: Identification of the tendon/ligament stem cell in mice and humans
papers.summary: The tendon/ligament stem cell is identified, and dysregulation of differentiation in this cell is shown as a mechanism contributing to lumbar spinal stenosis.

papers.title: An enzyme-responsive nanoplatform rewires host-microbe tryptophan metabolism for cancer immunotherapy
papers.summary: An oral enzyme-responsive co-delivery nanoplatform is designed to achieve controlled release of tryptophan and the metabolism inhibitor NLG919, specifically in the large intestine. This design redirects tryptophan metabolism toward immunostimulatory microbial indole derivative production, while blocking the immunosuppressive kynurenine pathway, thereby synergistically eliciting robust antitumor immunity in colorectal cancer.

papers.title: Myo-inositol metabolism counteracts mycotoxin hijacking and confers broad resistance to fungal diseases in crops
papers.summary: Xia et al. reveal that the Fusarium mycotoxin DON hijacks host central metabolism through NAD+-dependent enzymes to promote disease and identify MIPS as a key safeguard that redirects myo-inositol metabolism to drive PI(4,5)P2-dependent vacuolar sequestration of DON, maintaining metabolic homeostasis and conferring broad Fusarium resistance in crops.

papers.title: A commensal-derived sugar protects against obesity by regulating immunometabolism
papers.summary: Tan et al. identify a human commensal bacterium, Clostridium immunis—and its bioactive phosphocholine-modified exopolysaccharide (EPS)—that reduces visceral adiposity and weight gain in mice. By decreasing IL-22 levels, this EPS increases metabolic activity specifically in visceral fat. Metagenomic analyses suggest that this bacterial pathway may be conserved in humans.

papers.title: Dietary pectin remodels commensal bacterial surfaces to promote IgA-mediated protection from intestinal inflammation
papers.summary: Tang et al. reveal that dietary pectin drives Bacteroides uniformis surface remodeling to enrich the surface glycosphingolipid HexCer. Neutrophils sense this signal via CLEC4E to promote IgA production, which helps this bacterium colonize the gut lining and protects against colitis, uncovering a diet-microbe pathway that promotes a mutually beneficial relationship.

papers.title: The rice circadian clock orchestrates the rhizosphere microbiome to synchronize nitrogen supply with plant demand
papers.summary: Enhancing nitrogen use efficiency (NUE) is pivotal for sustainable agriculture yet constrained by spatiotemporal N mismatches. Du et al. find that the rice circadian clock orchestrates rhizosphere microbes to synchronize N supply with demand. Clock component Nhd1 drives rhythmic root exudation to regulate microbial N turnover, enhancing grain yield and NUE.

papers.title: Microbial indole-3-acetamide alleviates polycystic ovary syndrome through HIF-2α-ceramide signaling
papers.summary: Chen et al. reveal that C. aerofaciens mitigates PCOS pathology through activation of the adipose HIF-2α-ceramide signaling pathway. C. aerofaciens activates this pathway through production of indole-3-acetamide (IAM). Construction of an engineered probiotic strain expressing IAM synthase to stably produce IAM shows therapeutic efficacy in a mouse PCOS model.

papers.title: Hippuric acid metabolism by Corynebacterium glucuronolyticum-like bacteria promotes calcium oxalate crystallization
papers.summary: Qi et al. identify Corynebacterium glucuronolyticum-like (C. glucuronolyticum-like) bacteria enriched in the urine of calcium oxalate (CaOx) stone patients and show that they promote CaOx crystallization through hippuric acid degradation and biofilm formation. Hippuric acid or cranberry prevents C. glucuronolyticum-like bacteria-driven crystallization, providing a microbiota-based preventive strategy.

papers.title: A microbial chromatin remodeler drives gastric cancer progression and immune evasion by reprogramming the host epigenome
papers.summary: Xie et al. reveal that Streptococcus anginosus promotes gastric immune evasion via extracellular vesicles that deliver a bacterial chromatin remodeler to host cells, co-opting TEAD1 to upregulate ZDHHC11 and stabilize PD-L1 through palmitoylation. Targeting this axis potentiates anti-PD-1 therapy, offering a potential strategy to improve immunotherapy in SA-positive gastric cancer.

papers.title: Bacteroides acidifaciens enriched by KRAS mutation promotes colorectal tumorigenesis
papers.summary: Jiao et al. identify Bacteroides acidifaciens as a bacterial pathogen that accumulates in CRC patients and mice harboring oncogenic mutant KRAS. B. acidifaciens selectively promotes the tumorigenesis of KRAS-mutant CRC via the SusF-ARHGEF2 axis, forming a positive feedforward signaling cascade. Targeting B. acidifaciens or SusF-ARHGEF2 crosstalk may suppress KRAS-mutant CRC progression.

papers.title: Distant lymph nodes compensate for resected tumor-draining lymph nodes during cancer immunotherapy
papers.summary: Menzel, Zhou, et al. examine the impact of surgical removal of tumor-draining lymph node (tdLN) resection on anti-tumor immunity. They find that after tdLN resection, tumor antigen is rerouted to distant LNs, where it supports tumor-specific T cell responses and immune checkpoint blockade efficacy. Targeting these compensatory LNs enhances anti-cancer immunity after lymph node surgery.

papers.title: Functional evaluation of TCR-pMHC pairs at scale allows in silico TCR reactivity prediction
papers.summary: Messemaker et al. develop a TCR rapid assembly platform (T-RAP) and use it to generate a large high-quality dataset of functionally validated TCR-pMHC pairs. With the resulting validated TCR-pMHC dataset (TCRvdb), structure-based prediction of TCR-pMHC reactivity is more feasible than previously assumed.

papers.title: Glucose-deprived tumor microenvironment activates AMP-activated protein kinase to drive adoptively transferred T helper 9 cell senescence
papers.summary: Glucose deprivation in the solid tumor microenvironment impairs T cell persistence, but the mechanisms remain unclear. Fu et al. identified an AMPK-ZAK-NIK axis activated by glucose deprivation in Th9 cells that inhibits IL-9 secretion, triggering cell senescence and impaired persistence. ZAK targeting rejuvenates Th9 cells, consequently boosting the anti-tumor potency of CAR-Th9-based therapies for solid tumors.

Aire is a cell-intrinsic regulator of natural IgM-secreting cells
papers.summary: The autoimmune regulator (Aire) promotes T cell tolerance through promiscuous gene expression in medullary thymic epithelial cells, but growing evidence suggests that it has functions beyond its canonical role in thymic tolerance. Sayed et al. demonstrate that Aire acts as a cell-intrinsic regulator of T-independent natural IgM-secreting cells, homeostatically restraining their number and natural IgM abundance.

papers.title: Microglia with distinct origins and non-canonical phenotypes coexist within the border-like niche of the brain’s circumventricular organs
papers.summary: Circumventricular organs are specialized brain regions lacking a blood-brain barrier. Van Hove et al. reveal that these regions harbor unique microglia and border-associated macrophage populations that respond to ageing and metabolism and are partly derived from fetal monocytes entering during a perinatal window, which can fully adopt the microglia identity.

papers.title: Targeting a site of vulnerability on circumsporozoite protein inhibits Plasmodium vivax malaria infection
papers.summary: Limited knowledge of protective B cell epitopes on the Plasmodium vivax circumsporozoite protein (PvCSP) remains a roadblock to vaccine development. Visweswaran et al. identify an inhibitory vaccine epitope on PvCSP that elicits antibodies capable of blocking sporozoite invasion of host hepatocytes. Definition of the structural basis for epitope recognition by a neutralizing antibody provides a roadmap for vaccine design.

papers.title: Germinal center interleukin-4 microniches drive tissue divergence of IgE memory B cell responses
papers.summary: IgE recall responses sustain allergic disease, but their anatomical regulation remains poorly understood. Villazala-Merino et al. identify Tfh cell-derived IL-4 microniches within germinal centers as an anatomical checkpoint that favors IgE recall responses in lymphoid organs while limiting their generation in the lung mucosa.

papers.title: Sensory neuronal mTORC1 kinase signaling establishes neuroimmune memory that initiates allergic immunity
papers.summary: How cumulative environmental allergen exposures are encoded by peripheral sensory neurons to shape immune responsiveness is unclear. Zhu et al. show that protease allergens induce an mTORC1-dependent, metabolically trained state in sensory neurons that amplifies later neuroimmune responses to allergens and enables cross-sensitization to antigenically distinct allergens.

papers.title: Cancers modulate processing and presentation of p53 neoantigens to evade T cell detection
papers.summary: Mutations in TP53 occur early in malignant transformation and are generally present in all descendant tumor cells. Haratani et al. find a dearth of actionable neoantigens displayed in the cancer immunopeptidome and define various mechanisms whereby tumor cells prevent effective processing and presentation of p53 neoantigens.

papers.title: Twenty-year persistence of SARS-CoV-1 immune imprinting shapes antibody responses to SARS-CoV-2 infection
papers.summary: Our understanding of long-term sarbecovirus immune imprinting remains limited. Zhang et al. reveal persistent imprinting in individuals sequentially infected with SARS-CoV-1 and SARS-CoV-2 over two decades, characterized by redirected antibody targeting from the variable receptor-binding motif to conserved receptor-binding domain (RBD) core regions after breakthrough infection. These findings define the durability and molecular basis of antibody imprinting and inform pan-sarbecovirus vaccine design.

papers.title: A pulmonary innate lymphoid cell-driven serotonergic neuroimmune axis orchestrates airway hyperreactivity and cough hypersensitivity
papers.summary: ILC2s engage in bidirectional neuroimmune crosstalk that shapes diverse physiological functions, yet whether ILC2-mediated serotonergic signaling affects asthma pathophysiology remains unexplored. Luo et al. show that ILC2-derived serotonin promotes type 2 immunity and activates vagal sensory neurons, contributing to airway hyperreactivity, lung inflammation, and cough hypersensitivity upon RSV infection. These findings reveal an ILC2-neuron crosstalk in asthma pathophysiology.

papers.title: “The Hole”: Poetry Like a Gunshot Wound
papers.summary: Medicine trains clinicians in a particular silence. Through diagnosis, we medicalize the causes of suffering—contusion, laceration, hemorrhage—as though renaming anguish might contain it, keeping it from spilling out of charts and into our own lives. Operating room and ward become, ironically, fluent in the language of suppression. Yet the horrifically wounded body insists on poetry. It is precisely here, in the rupture between what medicine measures and what human beings experience, that the poem becomes not decoration but necessity. In “The Hole,” poetry does not resolve this rupture or even fix the wound, in this case a gunshot to the patient’s head, another in an epidemic of harm. Instead, it plumbs the unspeakable, not by translating it into medical terminology but exposing the violence of what resists translation. papers.title: Intra-Arterial Alteplase After Successful Thrombectomy for Acute Ischemic Stroke—Reply

The amendment was implemented on February 10, 2025, after enrollment of 283 patients, of whom 214 had completed or were eligible for 90-day follow-up. No interim analyses had been conducted, and no outcome data by treatment group were available at the time of the amendment; therefore, the change was not informed by accumulating trial results.

papers.title: Review of Prepregnancy Care and Counseling
papers.summary: To the Editor I appreciate the expanded women’s health learning opportunities provided by the JAMA Network journals under the editorial leadership of Linda Brubaker, MD, MS. The comprehensive Review of prepregnancy care and counseling by Dr Cooper and colleagues will be a valuable resource for clinicians caring for women of reproductive age. I am curious whether the authors recommend preconception screening for hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection. The US Preventive Services Task Force, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists recommend screening for HCV infection. Curative antiviral treatment for HCV infection is available.

papers.title: Review of Prepregnancy Care and Counseling
papers.summary: To the Editor In reading the otherwise comprehensive article by Dr Cooper and colleagues on prepregnancy care and counseling, we were surprised by the lack of discussion about testing for iron deficiency. Iron deficiency, the world’s most common micronutrient deficiency, is epidemic in young women. Studies of healthy reproductive-aged female patients report that iron deficiency is present in approximately 38% using a ferritin cutoff of 30 μg/L. Questioning for the most frequent etiology, heavy menstrual bleeding, is often absent, and symptoms are frequently normalized and marginalized. We characterized neutralizing activity against SARS-CoV-2, HIV-1, and influenza viruses in ART-treated, virologically suppressed individuals spanning distinct CD4+ T-cell levels. BA.5 was the dominant SARS-CoV-2 neutralization target across CD4 strata, whereas D614G neutralization increased with greater immune reconstitution. This gradient was largely absent for the antigenically divergent NB.1.8.1 and XFG variants. HIV-1 neutralization was inversely associated with CD4+ T-cell count, while influenza showed strain-dependent patterns. Neutralization-to-protection bridging preserved a CD4-associated gradient for D614G but not for highly immune-evasive variants. papers.title: Beyond HCD: complementary fragmentation chemistries expand HLA class I immunopeptidome discovery
papers.summary: Mass spectrometry based immunopeptidomics is limited by peptide identification. HLA class I ligands are non-tryptic, frequently carry low charge states and often fragment incompletely, yet nearly all workflows rely on a single activation method, higher-energy collisional dissociation (HCD). Unlike proteomics, where a protein is inferred from several peptides, in immunopeptidomics the peptide is itself the analyte and the candidate therapeutic target, so a ligand that is not identified is a target that is not found. Here we evaluate whether two alternative activation chemistries, ion trap collision-induced dissociation (CID) and infrared multiphoton dissociation (IRMPD), recover ligands that HCD does not. To our knowledge this is the first application of either method to HLA class I immunopeptidomics, made practical by the integrated infrared laser of the Orbitrap Tribrid Apex MultiOmics. papers.title: ClonoDynamics enables replicate-resolved inference of longitudinal T cell receptor repertoire dynamics
papers.summary: Longitudinal T cell receptor repertoire analysis can confound biological change with measurement noise and estimator-induced structure. We developed ClonoDynamics, a framework integrating latent abundance inference with replicate-decoupled estimates of directional change and cross-replicate displacement covariance. Pseudo longitudinal series assembled from 12 independently processed technical measurements of one biological sample revealed apparent restoring dynamics caused by reusing measurements for conditioning and change estimation. Separating these roles between replicates largely removed this artifact. Synthetic controls preserving empirical detection patterns showed dose-dependent recovery of temporal accumulation, resolving the two larger imposed effects but not the smallest. papers.title: Tumor cell-intrinsic mtDNA instability drives cGAS-dependent temporal remodeling of the melanoma immune microenvironment
papers.summary: Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) instability is an emerging feature of cancer, yet its biological effects on the tumor microenvironment (TME) and tumor progression remain incompletely defined. Using melanocyte-specific conditional silencing of mitochondrial transcription factor A (TFAM) in an autochthonous BrafV600E/Pten-/- melanoma model, we demonstrate that tumor cell-intrinsic mtDNA instability accelerates melanoma growth and metastatic dissemination in a cGAS-dependent manner. Transcriptomic profiling of early and late tumor stages revealed that mtDNA instability drives temporal remodeling of the tumor microenvironment (TME), characterized by an early type I interferon (IFN)-rich inflammatory state that licenses immunoregulatory programs as tumors progress. papers.title: CD24-dependent innate immune checkpoint targeting chimera disrupts TGF-β-driven immunosuppression to enhance anti-tumor therapy
papers.summary: The immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) poses formidable challenges for cancer immunotherapies. Among the complex TME landscape, the cytokine TGF-{beta}1 is an attractive soluble target for reinvigoration of anti-tumor immunity due to its pivotal function in immune cell suppression, extracellular matrix remodeling, and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) promotion, while immune checkpoint receptors exemplified by PD-1 and CD24 are promising surface targets. Though adaptive immune checkpoint inhibition is well established in clinical practice, TGF-{beta} blockade or innate immune checkpoint blockade is yet to be harnessed for tumor treatment. papers.title: Distinct Longitudinal Antibody Responses Following Primary Influenza Infection or Vaccination in Infants: A Prospective Birth Cohort Study
papers.summary: The longitudinal effects of initial influenza exposure on the magnitude, persistence, and antigen specificity of antibody responses during infancy remain incompletely understood. We investigated humoral antibody responses following primary influenza infection or seasonal vaccination in a prospective US birth cohort with weekly respiratory surveillance for influenza infection. Influenza-specific serum IgG binding to H1 and H3 haemagglutinin (HA) antigens, HA inhibition (HAI), and live-virus neutralizing antibody responses were assessed longitudinally. To minimize influence of maternally derived antibodies, analyses of primary exposure responses were restricted to infants for whom influenza-specific maternal antibodies had declined below the assay detection limit before exposure. Antibody responses were compared following primary infection and vaccination and examined after subsequent annual vaccination. We found that maternal influenza-specific IgG declined rapidly during early infancy.

papers.title: Sexual dimorphism in adult zebrafish marrows regulates blood cell composition and immune response
papers.summary: Hematopoiesis sustains lifelong blood production and immunity and is strongly influenced by biological sex. Males and females differ in their hematopoietic composition and susceptibility to infection and hematologic disease. Because current models cannot readily disentangle the independent contributions of sex chromosomes versus hormones, the mechanisms underlying sexual dimorphism remain poorly understood. Zebrafish have proven to be a powerful, translatable system for studying hematopoiesis, and offer a unique opportunity to isolate hormonal contributions due to their absence of sex chromosomes. However, whether sex is regulated in the zebrafish hematopoietic system remained unknown. Here, we discovered pronounced sexual dimorphism in the adult zebrafish marrow, with compositional differences peaking at reproductive age. papers.title: Lysophosphatidylserine Nanoparticles Induce Oral Tolerance Independent of TIM-4 and Canonical PS Processing
papers.summary: Protein replacement therapy is highly effective for treating many protein-deficiency disorders, but its long-term clinical benefit is often limited by anti-drug antibody responses that neutralize therapeutic proteins, compromising safety and efficacy. To address these unwanted immune responses, a lipid nanoparticle-based immunotherapy platform has been developed to induce antigen-specific tolerance. Mice treated with antigen associated with either double-chain phosphatidylserine (PS) or lysophosphatidylserine (LysoPS), a single-acyl-chain phospholipid, showed reduced antibody titers following subcutaneous pre-exposure. However, only LysoPS nanoparticles induced tolerance after oral administration, suggesting structural differences between PS and LysoPS can impact tolerogenic potential, depending on the site of delivery. papers.title: Inflammation-induced of Clec18a inhibits immune responses via Trpm7-dependent Cbl activation
papers.summary: Innate immune responses must be tightly controlled to maintain immuno-homeostasis. However, the regulatory mechanisms underlying the activation and early stages of the innate immune response remain poorly defined. Here, we found the soluble C-type lectin Clec18a is up-regulated in multiple inflammatory diseases, including sepsis and influenza, and secreted within minutes upon activation in multiple immune cells, including macrophages, dendritic cells (DCs), and T cells. Clec18a-myeloid-knockout mice exhibited reduced survival and exacerbated inflammation than the wild-type. However, exogenous recombinant Clec18a administration alleviated inflammation both in vitro and in vivo. Mechanistically, we identified macrophage-inducible C-type lectin (Mincle) as the receptor of Clec18a. papers.title: Provisional extracellular matrix signaling network regulates tumor lymphoneogenesis and response to immunotherapy
papers.summary: Tertiary lymphoid structures (TLS) predict response to checkpoint inhibition, and conventional dendritic cells (cDC) are required to build and maintain them. What renders a niche permissive for their assembly is unknown: chemokines recruit the cellular constituents but do not specify how they organize. Here we show that the organizing signal is a matrix fragment. Proteolysis of the proteoglycan versican (VCAN) releases the matrikine versikine, constitutively in germinal center light zones and inducibly in tumor stroma. Versikine activates CD11b+ cDC and expands cDC1 to assemble TLS-archetypal triads, apposed DC: CD4+ T: CD8+ T units. Versikine-conditioned DC engage progenitor-exhausted CD8+ T cells (Tpex) and Th1-polarized follicular helper CD4+ T cells. papers.title: TGFB1-Engineered Induced Mesenchymal Stromal Cells Exhibit High Immunomodulatory Potency and Durably Reprogram Synovial Macrophages in Osteoarthritis
papers.summary: Clinical translation of mesenchymal stromal cell (MSC) therapies derived from primary tissue sources is limited by manufacturing inconsistencies driven by donor-to-donor variability, which reduces predictability of clinical response. Induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived MSCs (iMSCs) offer a promising donor-independent, clonal alternative strategy that is also more amenable to engineering, but whether engineered iMSCs reproduce the potency attributes of primary MSCs remains unclear. Here, we benchmarked a doxycycline-inducible, hTERT-immortalized iMSC line engineered to overexpress TGFB1 (TGFB1-iMSCs), a key regulator of macrophage polarization, against multiple adipose tissue-derived MSC (MSC(AT)) donors across predefined immunomodulatory and angiogenic potency attributes. TGFB1-iMSCs were smaller and more circular with comparable or higher proliferative rates than primary MSC(AT) donors. papers.title: A loopless subdomain of transferrin binding protein B can elicit a broadly cross-reactive humoral immune response targeting variants from both encapsulated and non-typeable Haemophilus influenzae
papers.summary: Haemophilus influenzae is a Gram-negative bacterium that causes pneumonia, otitis media, and invasive infections such as meningitis and bacteremia. A vaccine that confers protection against disease caused by H. influenzae serotype b is currently available and is highly effective, but infections caused by non-b serotypes and non-typeable strains are still prevalent and increasing, suggesting a need for a broadly cross-protective vaccine that will protect against infection by all H. influenzae strains. To address the need for broad cross-protection, this study focused on the surface lipoprotein component of the bipartite bacterial transferrin receptor, transferrin binding protein B (TbpB), which is universally present H. influenzae, irrespective of encapsulation status, and is essential for bacterial colonization and pathogenesis. papers.title: Distinct synovial fluid B-cell differentiation and activation profiles in rheumatoid arthritis
papers.summary: CD11c+CD21- B cells are overrepresented in rheumatoid arthritis (RA). Here we delineate their functional state at site of inflammation and its molecular basis. Phenotypic profiling of paired blood and synovial fluid from patients with anti-citrullinated protein antibody (ACPA) seropositive RA (N=12), seronegative RA (N=10) and spondyloarthritis (N=8), demonstrated a striking enrichment of CD11c+CD21- B cells in synovial fluid in all three diseases (average of CD19+ cells: 67%, 49% and 51%). In ACPA-positive RA we identified increased proportions of CD11c+IgG+CD27low cells and several stages of pre-plasmablasts. The CD11c+CD21- cells had a phenotype indicating BCR activation, proliferation, and antigen presentation. This B-cell profile was mirrored by a LAG3+CTLA4+TIGIT+ peripheral helper T-cell program in ACPA-positive RA, contrasting a CCR6+ Th17-skewing in seronegative RA. papers.title: Profiling of intestinal T cells reveals antigen-specific dependency on early-life programming for the generation of microbiota-reactive Tregs
papers.summary: The generation of appropriate responses to the intestinal microbiota is an essential aspect of immune homeostasis. Studies of microbes that elicit stereotyped, antigen-specific CD4 T cell responses support the view that immune recognition of the microbiota is specific, relatively limited, and largely skewed toward Tregs, but recent profiling efforts have suggested that recognition of the microbiota may be broader and less regulatory. Such studies have mostly tracked responses to single antigens or used mice that acquire their microbiota after weaning, which has made it difficult to generalize the rules that govern microbiota-mediated T cell responses. Here we comprehensively profile, for the first time, the T cell response to the microbiota at homeostasis, and develop a panel of tools to track multiple, endogenous microbiota-reactive CD4 T cell populations in vivo. papers.summary: Abstract Background: Experimental models that retain endogenous tumor immune complexity are needed to investigate heterogeneous responses to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) in melanoma. We established patient-derived melanoma organoids (PDMOs) to examine retention of parental tumor cellular components and investigate patient-specific and context-dependent responses to checkpoint blockade. Methods: Fresh melanoma specimens (n=50), including primary tumors, neoadjuvant-treated tumors and tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL) associated samples were processed for Matrigel-embedded culture of patient-derived melanoma organoids (PDMOs). Characterization and functional studies were performed in subsets of established cultures. papers.title: MHC restriction is structurally encoded by the T cell receptor germline
papers.summary: MHC restriction -- the requirement for {beta} T cell receptors (TCRs) to recognize Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) molecules when presenting peptide antigens -- is a pillar of adaptive immunity. Here, we provide direct structural evidence for TCR germline-encoded recognition of MHC molecules irrespective of antigenic peptide. We engineered "germline-like" TCRs to eliminate CDR3 specificity for peptide, and a molecular clamping strategy to trap ultra-low-affinity complexes with peptide-MHC for cryo-EM. We find that germline-like TCR/pMHC docking modes are identical to wild-type T cell receptors with intact CDR3 loops, across distinct peptide antigens and MHC alleles. Analysis of human TCR repertoires reveals enrichment of specific V genes and V-V{beta} pairing patterns associated with HLA-A*02 contexts. Thus, the TCR germline encodes the blueprint for MHC restriction, providing a sequence-based framework that could inform computational and AI-driven prediction of TCR specificity.

papers.title: HIV-1 prime-boost vaccination shapes distinct clonal trajectories and memory precursor states of Env- and Gag-specific T cells
papers.summary: Despite decades of HIV-1 vaccine development, the clonal and cellular determinants of durable vaccine-induced T cell memory remain incompletely understood. Here, we combined antigen-specific T cell receptor (TCR) identification, longitudinal TCR sequencing, and single-cell multi-omics to characterize Env- and Gag-specific memory precursor T cells elicited by the HIV Vaccine Trials Network (HVTN) 505 DNA prime-recombinant adenovirus serotype 5 (rAd5) boost (DNA/rAd5) vaccine regimen. We developed a generalizable high-throughput approach to identify HIV-1 Env- and Gag-specific TCRs and found distinct patterns of clonal expansion, persistence, and contribution to memory between Env- and Gag-specific CD8 T cell responses. The DNA prime and rAd5 boost differentially shaped these repertoires, with rAd5-induced clones contributing proportionally more to the Gag-specific than to the Env-specific memory precursor compartment. papers.title: Subclinical hepatorenal biomarker alterations and urogenital indicators in Schistosoma haematobium-infected School-Aged Children in Sene West District, Ghana
papers.summary: Urogenital schistosomiasis, caused by Schistosoma haematobium, remains a major public health challenge among school-aged children in rural Ghana. Although urogenital indicators are well-established, systemic hepatic biomarker alterations in post-mass drug administration pediatric settings remain poorly characterized. This cross-sectional study evaluated point-of-care urinalysis profiles alongside a panel of serum hepatic and renal biomarkers in 174 children (aged 3 to 16 years) from the Sene West District, Ghana. Active infection (urine microscopy egg detection) was identified in 84 participants (48.3%, median egg count = 4.50 eggs/10 mL, IQR: 1.00 - 9.25). Active infection was strongly associated with microhematuria (57.1% vs. 11.1%, p < 0.001), proteinuria (42.9% vs. 22.2%, p = 0.004), and leukocyturia (27.4% vs. 4.4%, p < 0.001). papers.title: Real-time situational assessment of respiratory virus epidemics in Australia over winter 2025 and an out-of-season influenza A H3N2 epidemic
papers.summary: Introduction: In temperate regions, influenza and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) typically exhibit seasonal epidemics during the winter months, often concurrently with SARS-CoV-2 epidemics. Monitoring past and real-time trends in infection dynamics is important for informing public health situational awareness, including identifying and characterising unusual epidemic activity. However, data used to monitor these trends can exhibit substantial noise including strong day-of-the-week variation in reporting. In addition, case data for influenza can obscure distinct trends in influenza subtypes if not combined with virological data. papers.title: Parametric Models for Predicting Gram-negative Antibiotic Susceptibility Phenotype: A Brief Report
papers.summary: Predicted probabilities of antibiotic susceptibility to known or suspected pathogens can be used to support antibiotic selection. Patient demographic, clinical, and prior microbiologic history can be used to generate location-specific prediction models. For three Canadian tertiary care institutions we fit and evaluated models for predicting Gram-negative antibiotic susceptibilities to common antimicrobial agents based on previously established model structures. A web-based application was developed to permit visualization of antibiotic susceptibility predictions and support antibiotic decision-making.

papers.title: VSV-EBOV vaccination induces cross-reactive T-cell responses against Bundibugyo virus in humans
papers.summary: Bundibugyo ebolavirus (BDBV) is causing an ongoing outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) with no licensed vaccine available. Recent reports have shown the presence of BDBV-cross-reactive antibody responses in humans vaccinated against the related Ebola virus (EBOV). Here, we used an IFN-{gamma} ELISpot assay to assess T cell responses against the EBOV, BDBV and SUDV glycoproteins in clinical trial participants vaccinated with the licensed VSV-EBOV vaccine. We could show that BDBV-cross-reactive T cell responses are detectable in the majority of individuals and that conserved regions within the glycoprotein are targeted. In the absence of a BDBV-specific vaccine, these data support efficacy trials of the VSV-EBOV vaccine during the current outbreak.

papers.title: Correlates of Protection and Response Durability of the RTS,S Vaccine in Four Malaria Challenge Studies
papers.summary: RTS,S/AS01 (RTS,S) is one of two WHO-recommended malaria vaccines for children in moderate-to-high transmission settings. Yet, no validated immune correlate of protection (CoP) has been established for this vaccine. We selected 16 biomarkers to further assess as candidate CoPs, based largely on their ability to well-predict post-challenge outcomes in a previous integrative correlates analysis of two phase 2a controlled human malaria infection (CHMI) studies, Malaria-068 and Malaria-071. We evaluated the predictive power of these 16 biomarkers in two additional phase 2a CHMI studies, Malaria-092 and Malaria-102, to confirm these candidate CoPs in new malaria vaccine trials. In MAL092, malaria-naive volunteers were challenged three months after a series of two or three doses of RTS,S/AS01, and in MAL102, a subset were boosted nine months later and re-challenged after three weeks. papers.title: Persistent Borrelia burgdorferi protein antigen in CD16⁺ monocytes is associated with monocyte-skewed immune dysregulation in post-treatment Lyme disease syndrome (PTLDS)
papers.summary: Post-treatment Lyme disease syndrome (PTLDS) is characterized by persistent symptoms after antibiotic therapy for Borrelia burgdorferi infection. The mechanisms underlying these symptoms remain incompletely understood and have been attributed to ongoing low-level infection, autoimmunity, or immune dysregulation driven by residual bacterial antigens. We investigated whether Borrelia burgdorferi protein antigen persists in long-lived monocyte subsets in PTLDS patients and is associated with broader immune dysregulation. CD14CD16 monocytes from 10 patients with PTLDS were analyzed by mass spectrometry; plasma from all 10 was profiled on a 14-plex cytokine panel against 50 healthy donors; PBMCs from 6 patients (3 antigen-positive and 3 antigen-negative) underwent RT-qPCR and bulk RNA-seq with immune-compartment profiling. papers.title: Incidence and factors associated with infections in kidney transplant recipients at the tertiary hospital, Thailand.
papers.summary: In medical practice, the rising prevalence of infections in kidney transplant recipients (KTRs) is a notable concern. However, understanding the incidence and risk factors associated with infections in KTRs remains limited. This study aims to assess the incidence and factors associated infection among KTRs. Additionally, we also investigate the median time of each infection among KTRs. A retrospective cohort study was conducted from 1 January 2018-31 December 2022 at Thailands tertiary hospital. We performed univariable and multivariable logistic regression analyses to identify potential risk factors related infection and investigated for the incidence and median time of each infection among KTRs. papers.title: Genomic epidemiology reveals post-vaccine re-emergence of vaccine-associated G1P rotavirus lineages with variable disease severity
papers.summary: Group A rotavirus G1P[8] strains, which are targeted by the Rotarix vaccine, have persisted in several countries following the introduction of the Rotarix vaccine. However, the evolutionary origins of the persisting strains remain unclear. Here, we leveraged over two decades of rotavirus surveillance data from Malawi to understand the genomic epidemiology of G1P[8] strains in a high-disease-burden sub-Saharan African setting. We observed a reversion of G1P[8] strains to the conventional Wa-like genotype constellation identified pre-vaccination, following transient circulation of DS-1-like G1P[8] strains. Most G1P[8] lineages that re-emerged post-vaccination circulated before vaccine introduction. Furthermore, new strains emerged post-vaccination through re-assortment of pre-existing viruses. papers.summary: PurposeLong COVID literature often describes new-onset symptoms or conditions following SARS-CoV-2 infection; however, Long COVID also encompasses the exacerbation of pre-existing conditions. We describe health conditions reportedly worsened by COVID-19 illness and associated concerns in U.S. adults. MethodsWe collected longitudinal data from adults 18 years and older participating in the Track Post COVID-19 Conditions, an active Long COVID cohort surveillance project. Respondents completed surveys 3-, 6-, and 12- months after COVID-19 illness, beginning in July 2023. In each survey, respondents were asked whether they had any health conditions or concerns that were made worse by COVID-19. papers.title: A mechanistic framework for interpreting blood-stage malaria vaccine efficacy
papers.summary: Blood-stage vaccines (BSVs) against malaria offer a promising avenue for reducing parasite burden and transmission, yet their efficacy is challenging to interpret across different trial phases. In this study we develop a simple mechanistic within-host mathematical model of Plasmodium falciparum asexual parasitaemia. We fit this model to individual-level data from the phase I/IIa RH5.1 trial and estimate the relationship between vaccine efficacy and RH5 antibody titres, enabling the quantitative prediction of vaccine-impact on public health outcomes. We show that small reductions in erythrocyte invasion rate can lead to substantial decreases in probability of exceeding parasitaemia thresholds and transmission potential. Our framework provides a flexible, biologically motivated method for interpreting early-phase trial data and can inform future trial design, vaccine evaluation and integration into broader malaria control strategies.

papers.title: Integrated CRISPR-based detection of HIV, tuberculosis, malaria, and resistance-associated variants
papers.summary: HIV, tuberculosis (TB) and malaria are major infectious diseases that frequently co-circulate in high-burden settings, yet their diagnostic pathways remain largely disease-specific, complicating detection of coinfection and integration of antimicrobial-resistance testing. Here we developed HTM CARMEN, a highly multiplexed CRISPR-Cas13a molecular-testing framework that integrates detection of HIV-1, HIV-2, four Plasmodium species and Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) with detection of isoniazid-resistance-associated inhA and katG variants. We find that HTM CARMEN retained target selectivity and single-nucleotide discrimination across in vitro experiments and clinically relevant sample matrices, including whole blood, serum, sputum and dried blood spots. papers.title: Amplicon-based targeted next generation sequencing (tNGS) for Mycobacterium tuberculosis - unpacking the 'black box'
papers.summary: The WHO recently endorsed two commercial culture-free targeted next-generation sequencing (tNGS) assays for detecting drug resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis. These proprietary tNGS platforms present a black box. We developed an in-house tNGS assay using Oxford Nanopore Technology sequencing to detect an expanded range of resistance mutations directly from clinical specimens. The assay targeted 44 genomic loci; hsp65 for Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC) identification; 12 loci for MTBC lineage classification; and 31 drug resistance loci predicted resistance to 16 anti-TB drugs. In total, 98 amplicons were distributed across three PCR pools. papers.title: Genomic Epidemiology and Genetic Relatedness of Antimicrobial-Resistant Morganella morganii in Community and Hospital Settings in Bangladesh
papers.summary: Morganella morganii is an opportunistic pathogen with intrinsic and acquired antimicrobial resistance, but its genomic epidemiology remains poorly characterized in Bangladesh. We sequenced and compared genomes of 47 stool-derived M. morganii isolates from hospital (n = 29) and community (n = 18) participants in urban Dhaka. Susceptibility testing showed frequent resistance to imipenem (70{middle dot}2%) and cefuroxime (97{middle dot}9%), while all isolates were resistant to colistin. Resistance to meropenem (6{middle dot}4%) and ertapenem (2{middle dot}1%) was uncommon. Based on acquired non-susceptibility across tested antimicrobial categories, 18/47 (38{middle dot}3%) isolates were multidrug-resistant, including 15/29 (51{middle dot}7%) hospital-derived and 3/18 (16{middle dot}7%) community-derived isolates. papers.title: Spatiotemporal clustering of tuberculosis notifications in Nepal during the COVID-19 pandemic and subsequent recovery: A national space-time scan analysis, 2019-2024
papers.summary: The COVID-19 pandemic substantially disrupted tuberculosis (TB) prevention, diagnosis, and treatment services worldwide. Despite increased TB notifications in Nepal during the post-pandemic recovery period, the geographic distribution and temporal clustering of notifications remain poorly understood. This study examined the spatial and temporal patterns of TB notifications across Nepal during the COVID-19 recovery period. We conducted a nationwide retrospective ecological analysis of district-level TB notifications across all 77 districts of Nepal from FY 2019/20 to FY 2023/24. Space-time, purely spatial, and purely temporal scan statistics were performed using a discrete Poisson model in SaTScan. Statistical significance was assessed using Monte Carlo simulation with 999 replications. A total of 172,155 TB cases were notified during the study period. papers.title: Diagnostic information from a negative QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus result in adults evaluated for tuberculosis in Brazil and South Africa
papers.summary: Interferon-gamma release assays detect Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection but cannot distinguish infection from active tuberculosis (TB). We evaluated the diagnostic information provided by QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus (QFT-Plus) among adults investigated for active TB in Brazil and South Africa. papers.summary: Nature Reviews Immunology, Published online: 28 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41577-026-01361-8 Immune-based therapies have transformed the treatment of cancer and inflammatory and autoimmune diseases, but treatment is often suboptimal and the ability to predictably harness the immune system for new therapies remains limited. The pharmacology of immune-based drugs may be distinct from that of many traditional therapies. Here, I outline four principles of ‘immunopharmacology’ that provide a framework for understanding how the immune system responds to therapeutic perturbation. These principles may help to better define how immune-based therapies work and identify new opportunities for drugging the immune system.

papers.title: ‘Trained’ sensory neurons drive allergic sensitization
papers.summary: Nature Reviews Immunology, Published online: 28 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41577-026-01362-7 A study in Immunity reports that protease allergens ‘train’ sensory neurons through metabolic remodelling to enhance the response to re-exposure.

papers.title: What the ‘negative space’ tells us about the immunology of multiple sclerosis
papers.summary: Nature Reviews Immunology, Published online: 28 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41577-026-01358-3 By exploring five enduring “negative spaces” in multiple sclerosis (MS) research, Kaufmann, Gold and Fugger challenge simple explanations of disease pathogenesis. Their Comment argues that MS emerges from complex interactions between immunity, infection and tissue resilience, offering a fresh framework for understanding progression and therapeutic intervention.

papers.title: The next big questions in immunology
papers.summary: Nature Reviews Immunology, Published online: 25 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41577-026-01353-8 As Nature Reviews Immunology marks its twenty-fifth anniversary, leading immunologists reflect on the questions, challenges and conditions that will shape the future of the field.

papers.title: Plasticity of the infant immune system during the perinatal period
papers.summary: Nature Reviews Immunology, Published online: 18 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41577-026-01354-7 Immune plasticity during the perinatal period enables mammalian offspring to successfully navigate the transition from prenatal, intrauterine life to postnatal, extrauterine life. This Review highlights recent advances in our understanding of perinatal immune plasticity and the factors that modulate it, with implications for neonatal health and disease.

papers.title: Publisher Correction: Immune surveillance and immune evasion of senescent cells
papers.summary: Nature Reviews Immunology, Published online: 17 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41577-026-01360-9 Publisher Correction: Immune surveillance and immune evasion of senescent cells

papers.title: Immunogenic cell death and tertiary lymphoid structures: bridging tumour cell death and immune organization
papers.summary: Nature Reviews Immunology, Published online: 16 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41577-026-01356-5 The formation of tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs) has been associated with better outcomes in patients with certain tumours. Here the authors discuss how immunogenic cell death can lead to the formation of TLSs and explain why this knowledge could help us design better cancer therapies.

papers.title: Cities cannot go green without soil microorganisms
papers.summary: Nature Reviews Microbiology, Published online: 02 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41579-026-01380-1 Urban soils must move from providing single, engineered functions to supporting multifunctionality. Managing their microbiomes could simultaneously strengthen climate regulation, water retention, pollutant removal, biodiversity and human health, but only if biological restoration is coupled to risk assessment, long-term monitoring and equitable access.

papers.title: How bacterial immune systems sense phage infection
papers.summary: Nature Reviews Microbiology, Published online: 02 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41579-026-01376-x Bacteria deploy diverse immune systems to counter phage infection, yet how these systems sense invasion remains incompletely understood. This Review categorizes phage-derived triggers and outlines emerging principles that govern immune recognition of phage infection.

papers.title: Microbial ecology of shallow groundwater ecosystems
papers.summary: Nature Reviews Microbiology, Published online: 01 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41579-026-01362-3 In this Review, Karwautz and Griebler examine the microbial communities found in shallow groundwater and aquifers, exploring their diversity, functional roles and dynamic interactions with adjacent terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems, as well as the influence of global change and anthropogenic pressures on these microorganisms.

papers.title: Microbial synthesis and degradation of bio-based biodegradable plastics
papers.summary: Nature Reviews Microbiology, Published online: 01 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41579-026-01370-3 In this Review, O’Connor and colleagues discuss the contributions of microorganisms across the life cycle of key bio-based polymers and assess the current role, the potential and limitations of microbial production and degradation of bio-based polymers as well as the implications for integration of microbiological processes into a circular bioeconomy.

papers.title: Rethinking soil microbiome interventions through an ecological lens
papers.summary: Nature Reviews Microbiology, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41579-026-01381-0 Microbial interventions offer sustainable opportunities to enhance soil health and ecosystem functioning, but they can also have unintended ecological consequences. This Comment explores their benefits and risks, arguing for a shift in perspective from microbial products as agricultural inputs to tools for ecological restoration.

papers.title: Bifidobacteria: biogeography, host adaptation and ecological functions
papers.summary: Nature Reviews Microbiology, Published online: 28 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41579-026-01367-y In this Review, van Sinderen and colleagues explore how bifidobacteria evolved as an important human gut symbiont, highlighting genomic adaptations, metabolic versatility, ecological interactions and host-modulatory functions.

papers.title: A four-way interaction in the rhizosphere
papers.summary: Nature Reviews Microbiology, Published online: 24 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41579-026-01379-8 This Genome Watch discusses recent evidence on the interactions among a plant, a fungal pathogen, its bacterial endosymbiont and the rhizosphere microbiome, highlighting how such multipartite relationships shape plant health and disease, with implications for crop productivity in an era of global change.

papers.title: After the rain in biocrusts
papers.summary: Nature Reviews Microbiology, Published online: 22 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41579-026-01378-9 This study shows that rewetting activates a small, distinct subset of dryland biocrust bacteria, with mature communities showing greater microbial activity independent of light conditions.
